issues.legal_issue: A delegated rule may make continued occupation of subsidised industrial housing subject to income-based eligibility conditions even when the occupant remains an industrial worker under the governing statute.
material_facts: The occupants had been allotted subsidised industrial houses and remained industrial workers, but their incomes exceeded the prescribed ceiling.
An amendment made continued eligibility to retain an allotted house subject to an income ceiling and provided for cancellation of the allotment.
The statute empowered the government to make rules concerning the manner of allotment and conditions of occupation, and provided for cancellation and treatment of occupants as unauthorised occupants.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was within the rule-making power and was not ultra vires the statute.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 24, including section 24(2)(ii) and (x), the government could prescribe the manner of allotment and conditions of occupation. Sections 7 and 9, including section 9(2), permit cancellation where an allottee ceases to meet prescribed conditions then in force and provide for treating the allottee as an unauthorised occupant. The statutory definition of an industrial worker in section 2(e) does not make allotment unconditional or prevent additional conditions on retaining housing.

predicates.challenge_to_industrial_housing_occupanc: A proceeding challenges a rule governing continued occupation of housing allotted under an industrial housing scheme.
predicates.delegated_authority_covers_occupation_co: The governing law authorizes the rule-maker to prescribe conditions relating to occupation of the housing.
predicates.rule_sets_condition_for_retaining_allott: The challenged rule makes an occupant's continued retention of allotted housing subject to a prescribed condition.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns an industrial housing occupancy rule, the law authorizes conditions of occupation, and the rule sets a condition for retaining the housing, the rule is within the delegated power.

issues.legal_issue: A rule requiring notice before cancellation of an existing housing allotment does not operate retrospectively merely because it links eligibility to an income threshold.
material_facts: The occupants had been allotted and were occupying industrial houses before the amendment took effect.

The amendment stated that an allottee whose income exceeded the threshold became ineligible, but its proviso required written notice before cancellation for occupants already in their houses when the amendment commenced.
The occupants were given notices under that proviso, and the court construed cancellation as taking effect after the notice period rather than from the date the income first exceeded the threshold.
issues.conclusion: The amendment did not operate retrospectively against existing occupants; their allotments could be cancelled only after the prescribed written notice.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to rule 4(3), read in the context of the amendment, means that an existing allotment is not cancelled from the date the income threshold is crossed but only after the written notice specified in the proviso. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_amended_eligibility_rule: A proceeding challenges an amendment that changes eligibility to retain allotted housing.
predicates.existing_occupant_before_amendment: The person held and occupied the allotted housing before the amendment commenced.
predicates.cancellation_requires_written_notice: The amendment requires written notice before cancellation of an existing allotment.

issues.definition: When an eligibility-rule challenge concerns a person already occupying the housing and cancellation requires written notice, cancellation of that existing allotment takes effect after notice.

issues.legal_issue: An equality challenge not raised in the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in the appeal, and cannot be considered while the relevant constitutional guarantee is suspended.
material_facts: The occupants argued in the appeal that the amendment arbitrarily discriminated against workers whose incomes exceeded the ceiling.
The equality contention had not been raised before the High Court.
At the time relevant to the appeal, a Presidential Order had suspended the operation of Article 14 during the specified emergency period.
issues.conclusion: The court did not permit the equality contention to be raised in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that the contention could not be raised at that stage because it had not been raised before the High Court and, independently, could not be allowed in view of the Presidential Order under Article 359(1) suspending Article 14. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and equality_claim_in_appeal and (equality_claim_not_raised_below or equality_guarantee_suspended)

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.equality_claim_in_appeal: A party raises an equality-based challenge to the measure in the appeal.
predicates.equality_claim_not_raised_below: The party did not raise that equality-based challenge before the lower court.
predicates.equality_guarantee_suspended: The constitutional equality guarantee invoked by the party is suspended at the relevant time.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a dismissed writ petition, an equality claim is not considered if it is raised in the appeal and was not raised below or the invoked equality guarantee is suspended.
